prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength are interrogated free of Doppler and recoil shifts, and for bringing it to a fractional uncertainty near 1e-18

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged in substance from round 1: B018 with Katori and Ye, and I now hold it with more confidence than in my opening ballot. The test I apply is whether this is an original invention, experimentally verified, that opens a door to something people could not see before. The magic-wavelength lattice is such an invention. Katori proposed the trapping principle, in which the light shifts of the two clock states cancel so that thousands of neutral atoms can be held in the Lamb-Dicke regime, and his group made the first strontium lattice clock. It is neither a frequency comb nor a single trapped ion, and it combines the statistics of an ensemble with the systematic control of a trapped particle. The result is verified in Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and elsewhere, on several species, with inter-laboratory comparisons, and it already shows things that were invisible before: gravitational redshift across millimetres, tighter limits on drifts of constants, and a basis for networks of clocks in geodesy and dark-matter searches. On the chair's question about Ye, I would credit him for taking the clock from a proposed scheme to a quantitatively understood many-body instrument with record accuracy and coherence, which is more than refinement because it showed that the lattice principle works at the 1e-18 level. I would not wait for the redefinition of the second, because the Nobel criterion is the discovery, and the demonstrated and compared accuracy already meets it. My preferred citation is deliberately worded around the lattice principle and its realisation, so that the distinction from 2005 and 2012 is on the page.
statement.case_against: I still see three real weaknesses and I do not want the support count to hide them. First, five of eight members now prefer B018, but three of us moved there after reading each other's openings, and I am one of them, so the count is weaker evidence than it looks. Second, the overlap with the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 trapped-ion prize is a real objection. Ye worked in the Hall environment, and a skeptical reader will say that the clock combines honoured tools. My answer, that the magic-wavelength lattice is a new trapping principle and a new route to stability, is a judgement I find convincing but not beyond argument. Third, my own rule is that the prize goes to the original experiment, not to the later and better realisation. Katori's concept and first demonstration meet that rule fully. Ye's share rests on the claim that his group's accuracy and many-body work was a decisive demonstration and not only a record, and on the evidence I have seen I accept that, but I cannot verify the record uncertainties myself and I would want an expert reviewer to confirm who achieved which milestone first. The contributions of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and the Yb and Hg groups lie outside two names, and that cannot be resolved by the three-name limit.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B038 (gamma-ray burst afterglows) as a mature discovery that resolved a thirty-year puzzle, concedes that the optical counterpart and redshift credit may sink the case, and lists B018 and B004 as alternatives. He is also unsure that the committee wants a second precision-measurement prize after 2005 and 2012.
responses.response: I agree that B038 is a real discovery and that the stability of its interpretation under Swift and Fermi is what I look for. My difficulty is the one you name yourself. I want to be absolutely sure that we have found the people who did the original work, and with an X-ray localisation by BeppoSAX, then an optical counterpart, then a redshift from several groups, I cannot map that onto three names without excluding people whose steps were decisive. If there were a way to confine the prize to the X-ray localisation with Costa and Frontera, I would take it more seriously, but that would not describe the cosmological origin, which is the discovery you want to honour. I also take your point on the earlier prizes. I do not think of this as a third precision prize in the same line, because the lattice clock rests on a trapping principle that neither 2005 nor 2012 contained. I keep B038 as an alternative for that reason, and I would support asking for an expert report on attribution before the final vote.

responses.point: Kroll asks whether the large magnetoresistance in later tunnel-junction devices came from Parkin's MgO work, so that a prize for the 1995 work alone would reward the opening step, and notes that for the lattice clock the opening idea and the decisive demonstrations sit with the same two groups. He also asks whether Ye's share is accuracy and many-body work or comb infrastructure.
responses.response: Your argument on B003 is the one that moved me, together with Mehlig's: the 1995 priority is clear, but the effect that made the technology came later and with different people, so a citation must either include Parkin and Butler and Mathon, which exceeds three names, or honour a step that is not the decisive one. I have therefore dropped it from my configuration. On Ye, I would define his share as the accuracy and coherence of the strontium lattice clock and the many-body work, and not as comb infrastructure, which was the content of the 2005 prize. That is why I want the citation to say that the clock was realised and brought to 1e-18, not only that it is accurate. I would ask you, as the member who knows the Boulder environment, whether you agree that this wording keeps comb credit out of Ye's share.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the scientific content of the lattice clock is not the number but the demonstration that a many-body ensemble of neutral atoms with controlled interactions can stay coherent long enough to resolve relativistic effects over millimetres. She asked how I compare this with tunnel magnetoresistance, which I ranked first in my opening.
responses.response: I accept your framing, and it answers the question I put to you in round 1: the physics is distinct and not only the performance, because the many-body coherence and the millimetre redshift measurement are new observations. As for tunnel magnetoresistance, I now rank it below the clock. It has the clearer societal benefit, but the combination of the 2007 GMR prize, Julliere's 1975 observation and the Parkin, Butler and Mathon credit problem makes it harder to be sure about who did the original work. The clock has a clean attribution and an observation that was not possible before. I still ask you to check that the wording of the citation does not claim the redshift measurement as Katori's and Ye's alone, since the JILA and Tokyo groups were each involved in the comparisons.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B012 (defect-mediated 2D melting) for Young, Halperin and Nelson, but says he could move if it looks like a sequel to 2016, lists B018 first among his alternatives, and separates Katori's concept from the accuracy campaign shared with Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and Hinkley.
responses.response: I take B012 seriously as science, and the long record of testing is attractive. It is, however, a theoretical result, and for a theory I would need decisive experimental support that has the same status as the prediction. As you say yourself, the colloidal and simulation evidence is system-dependent, with first-order melting in some cases, and the committee would have to say which systems show the two-step scenario. I cannot say that on the evidence in front of us. I also agree with your point that the accuracy campaign has more authors than two, but I read this as a feature of any experimental prize. The question for the citation is who made the decisive invention and demonstration, and the lattice, as you say, was Katori's. I would welcome your view on whether the citation I propose, which names the lattice principle first and the accuracy second, answers your separation of concept and campaign.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B044 (magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene) with MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer as a theory-plus-experiment trio, and argues that the pairing mechanism was also unsettled for the cuprates.
responses.response: The cuprate comparison is fair, and I do not require a settled mechanism. My concern is different. As a microscopist I trust the spectroscopy that supports the band picture, but the field has had about eight years, and the platform is still changing with the moire TMD systems, so it is hard to say what in the physical picture is mature enough to put into a citation. The credit also leaves out Cao and Fatemi, who did the original transport measurements, and the precursor theory, and in my view a first experimental discovery of correlated states without its first authors is the sort of credit that we should be sure about. I keep B044 as my first alternative and I would support it in a later year, but I would not choose it now over a candidate with a clean two-name credit.

uncertainties: Whether Ye's decisive demonstrations are separable from the comb infrastructure of the 2005 prize, which an expert reviewer should confirm by checking who first reached each accuracy milestone.
Whether the committee accepts the magic-wavelength lattice as a distinct trapping principle and not an extension of the 2005 and 2012 prizes. I believe it does, but this is a judgement.
Whether the clock record uncertainties and inter-laboratory comparisons are as I describe, since I rely on the opening statements and my own recall.
Whether the convergence on B018 reflects scientific judgment or the effect of reading each other's openings, since three of the five supporters moved there after the first round.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B018, B044 or B038. I have no known collaboration with Katori, Ye, Costa, Frontera, Kulkarni, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer. My Japanese academic ties (University of Tokyo fellowship, Kyushu, Tohoku and JSPS exchanges) are with the microscopy community and not with the clock groups, and I have disclosed them so colleagues can judge. Goran Johansson is a Chalmers colleague and Bernhard Mehlig is in the neighbouring Gothenburg department, which has no bearing on B018. No recusal is needed for my preferred configuration.
